108.subtitle: Marrow, the swan, turmeric-rice, and the letter ha

commentary.meaning: Four names close the sixth panel, the fewest the hymn has given to any of these goddesses. Three of the four begin with the same sound. Her attendant is Haṃsavatī, her food is haridrānna, and she is Hākinī, and the coincidence is not one the other panels share: the fifth yoginī's retinue, dish and name have nothing in common phonetically, nor the fourth's, nor the third's. Here the whole station is tuned to a single letter, and the letter is the one that the yogic handbooks write on a petal of this very wheel. The other movement in the verse is inward. The previous goddess was seated in bone; this one is seated in the marrow that the bone encloses, so the survey has now reached the innermost tissue but one. After this only the crown remains, where the counting stops and the hymn resorts to words like all-facing and every kind of food.
commentary.history:
Majjā is the sixth of the seven bodily constituents, the marrow, produced according to the medical texts out of bone and producing in its turn the generative essence that the seventh and last goddess will occupy. Placing this yoginī there completes a movement begun in the previous verse: bone and then what is inside the bone, the container and the contained, assigned to two goddesses in succession. The medical tradition also brings the contents of the skull under this heading, which sits well with a goddess stationed between the eyebrows, though the hymn says nothing about the fit and leaves the reader to notice it.

Haṃsavatī heads the attendants, and to see why she is named at all one has to know how the wheels and the alphabet are connected. In the standard yogic scheme the six wheels have four, six, ten, twelve, sixteen and two petals — fifty in all — and the fifty letters of the Sanskrit alphabet are distributed one to a petal, running from the four petals of the root support up to the two of the wheel between the brows. The last two letters in that reckoning are ha and the conjunct kṣa, which is conventionally appended at the end of the alphabet, and they belong to the two petals of this wheel. The attendant powers of the petals are named from their letters, and the hymn names the first of the pair and passes over the second. Once this is in view, the goddess's own name stops looking arbitrary: Hākinī is named from the letter written on the petal she sits on, and the section has been proceeding through the alphabet's end.

The swan in her name carries more than heraldry. Haṃsa is the goose or swan of Sanskrit poetry, credited in a stock conceit with the ability to drink the milk out of a mixture of milk and water and leave the water behind — the standard emblem of discrimination, which is a suitable thing to find stationed at the wheel called command. It is also a syllable. Read as ha and sa, the word is heard in the breath itself, ha going out and sa coming in, and the tradition calls this the unrecited recitation, a mantra the body performs some twenty-one thousand times a day without anyone deciding to. Reversed, the same two sounds give so'ham, that I am, which is why the swan became the emblem of the renunciate and why the highest grade of them is called paramahaṃsa. The Upaniṣads had already made the bird a figure for the self at large in the world, dwelling in the sky, in men, in the gods, in truth. All of that arrives with the name of a petal-goddess who is mentioned once and not described.

Haridrā is turmeric, and in Indian usage it is three things at once: a dye, a medicine, and a substance of auspiciousness. It colours the thread tied at a wedding, it is smeared on the bride, and the rice tinted yellow with it is what gets distributed at ceremonies and carried home. Rice cooked with turmeric is therefore not simply another dish in the series but the festive one, the plate that means a good occasion. The hymn gives it to the goddess of the wheel between the brows and marks the gift with a word it has used nowhere else in the section: ekarasikā, having one relish only. Every other yoginī is said to be pleased, or gladdened, or attached; this one is exclusive. Rasa, the noun behind rasikā, is among the most overworked words in Sanskrit — sap, flavour, the aesthetic savour of a poem, mercury in the alchemists, the first of the seven bodily constituents in the physicians — and a rasika in literary usage is a connoisseur, someone whose taste is educated enough to be narrow. The name says she has that kind of taste, and that it settles on one dish.

The closing name uses the same formula as the fourth panel: bearing the form of, rather than the mother and her own being that the third, fifth and last panels use. Whether the variation carries weight is doubtful, and the metre alone will account for it. What is not accidental is the sound. Haṃsavatī, haridrānna, Hākinī: the panel comes to rest three times on the same aspirate, the letter of its own petal, and it is the only one of the seven where the hymn does anything of the kind.

One station remains. The seventh goddess sits at the thousand-petalled lotus above the six, is not counted among the wheels that carry the alphabet, and receives no number of faces and no single dish — only the words for all directions and all food. The section that began at the throat with one face and a bowl of sweetened milk-rice will end by running out of things to count.
commentary.practice:
This verse breaks a habit the section has kept for ten verses. Every name so far has been four syllables or eight, and every one has fitted inside a quarter of the verse. Haṃsavatīmukhyaśaktisamanvitā is twelve syllables long and runs through the boundary between the second and third quarters, so the customary breath after the eighth syllable would fall in the middle of a word. The first line has to be carried in one span, and reciters settled into the section's rhythm are apt to be caught out.

Majjāsaṃsthā rewards being set beside the tissue-names of the earlier panels. Māṃsaniṣṭhā and medoniṣṭhā have the retroflex cluster ṣṭh; this one and asthisaṃsthitā have the dental sth. The difference is not a matter of taste. Niṣṭhā is ni plus sthā, and the i of the prefix pulls the s back into a retroflex ṣ, which then drags the following stop back with it; saṃsthā is sam plus sthā, and the vowel a does no such thing. One rule accounts for every instance in the section. The other thing in the word is the doubled jj, two palatal stops held long, tongue flat against the palate for both.

The long attendant-name is a chain of clusters: khya, an aspirated velar plus the palatal glide, in mukhya; kti in śakti; nvi in samanvitā. None is individually hard; the difficulty is stamina, so practise the word alone until it can be said through without a break.

Haridrānnaikarasikā contains two different vowel fusions and is the best single illustration of them in the hymn. Haridrā ends in a long ā and anna begins with a short a, and long plus short gives simply long ā. Then anna ends in a short a and eka begins with e, and a short a plus e gives the diphthong ai — which is why the word has nnai in the middle where nothing in its components suggests one. The previous verse showed the companion rule with mudga and odana producing au. Learn the pair together: a plus e gives ai, a plus o gives au, and a great many puzzling Sanskrit words come apart at once.

For archanā, three names take the ordinary feminine ending — majjāsaṃsthāyai, haṃsavatīmukhyaśaktisamanvitāyai, haridrānnaikarasikāyai — and the fourth, being an ī-stem, does not: hākinīrūpadhāriṇyai namaḥ. The first syllables of that name are long then short, hā then ki, and levelling them is the standard fault.

The verse gives the person chanting it two things to hold, and they pull in opposite directions. One is the marrow, the deepest and least accessible tissue in the body, the part no one has any sensation of, named as a place where the goddess lives. The other is the swan in the attendant's name, which is the breath going in and out of the reciter at that very moment. Between them the verse covers the whole distance from what is entirely hidden to what could not be more immediate, and it makes no distinction between the two as places to find her. Used in nyāsa, the verse is spoken with the hand at the point between the brows. Chanted straight through, it is over in ten seconds and leaves one station left.

crossReferences.source: Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.2 (the verse also stands in the Ṛgveda)

crossReferences.iast: haṃsaḥ śuciṣad vasur antarikṣasad dhotā vediṣad atithir duroṇasat | nṛṣad varasad ṛtasad vyomasad abjā gojā ṛtajā adrijā ṛtaṃ bṛhat ||
crossReferences.translation: The swan seated in the bright sky, the good one seated in the middle air, the priest seated at the altar, the guest seated in the house; seated in men, seated in the gods, seated in the truth, seated in space; born of water, born of cattle, born of truth, born of rock — the great truth.
crossReferences.relevance: The verse that made the swan a technical term. It is a list of seats, and its point is that one thing occupies all of them without becoming any of them — which is what the entire yoginī section is asserting, verse by verse, about skin and blood and flesh and bone and marrow. The Kaṭha's swan and the Haṃsavatī of this verse are the same bird, and the breath-mantra later heard in the word is a domestication of this claim rather than a departure from it.

crossReferences.deva: हिरण्यवर्णां हरिणीं सुवर्णरजतस्रजाम् । चन्द्रां हिरण्मयीं लक्ष्मीं जातवेदो म आ वह ॥
crossReferences.iast: hiraṇyavarṇāṃ hariṇīṃ suvarṇarajatasrajām | candrāṃ hiraṇmayīṃ lakṣmīṃ jātavedo ma ā vaha ||
crossReferences.translation: Gold-coloured, yellow, garlanded in gold and silver, bright as the moon, made of gold — bring Lakṣmī to me, O knower of all that is born.
crossReferences.relevance: Worth setting beside haridrānna because hariṇī and haridrā are the same colour word underneath: hari, the yellow-green of turmeric and of gold. The Vedic hymn asks for prosperity in the vocabulary of that colour, and turmeric occupies the same place in domestic practice, smeared on brides and stirred into the rice that is handed round at weddings. When the hymn gives yellow rice to a goddess and says she cares for nothing else, it is drawing on a very old association of that shade with a good outcome.

references.title: Vāc: The Concept of the Word in Selected Hindu Tantras
references.author: André Padoux, tr. Jacques Gontier (SUNY Press, 1990)
references.note: The indispensable book for the part of this verse that is hardest to see, namely that the wheels of the body are an alphabet before they are anything else. Padoux's chapters on the mātṛkā explain why fifty petals should carry fifty letters and why a goddess would be named from one of them, which is what makes sense of Haṃsavatī and Hākinī standing where they do.

references.title: Indian Food: A Historical Companion
references.author: K. T. Achaya (Oxford University Press, 1994)
references.note: The best history of what people in India have actually cooked and eaten, by a food scientist who read the Sanskrit sources. Read the entries on turmeric, rice preparations and pulses to see that the seven dishes distributed among these goddesses are an accurate cross-section of an ordinary repertoire, and that turmeric rice in particular carries a festive weight that the hymn is trading on.

references.title: The Serpent Power: The Secret of Tantra Yoga
references.author: Arthur Avalon (Sir John Woodroffe) (1919; Dover and Ganesh reprints)
references.note: Cited here for one thing only: the petal-by-petal tables of the wheels, which set out the four, six, ten, twelve, sixteen and two petals with their letters. The tables are reliable even where the surrounding exposition has dated badly, and they are the quickest way to confirm that ha sits on a petal of the wheel between the brows.

references.title: Tantric Visual Culture: A Cognitive Approach
references.author: Sthaneshwar Timalsina (Routledge, 2015)
references.note: A study of how tantric texts expect their images to be built up in the mind, written by someone trained in the tradition as well as in the academy. Useful at the end of this section for the question a reader is likely to be left with — what a practitioner is supposed to be doing when he installs a six-faced white goddess in his own skull and offers her yellow rice.
